sources.title: Predictive Representations of State
sources.author_label: M. L. Littman, R. S. Sutton and S. Singh

reviewed_source.edition: NIPS 2001 proceedings, volume 14, pp. 1555–1561; supplied 14-physical-page PDF
reviewed_source.attribution_note: All three authors are verified on the PDF title page; the proceedings HTML/BibTeX omits Singh. Physical PDF pages 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 are content pages 1–7 and proceedings pp. 1555–1561; every even physical page is blank.
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; public metadata and summaries do not redistribute the supplied PDF.

sources.application: Conceptual context: future-test probabilities motivate predictive state. Zenith’s implemented deterministic rational-linear learner is not the stochastic PSR construction or evidence of its proposed learning advantages.

source_locators.locator: §1, Eqs. (1)–(3); physical PDF pp. 5, 7 / content pp. 3–4 / proceedings pp. 1557–1558
source_locators.supports: A predictive state determines probabilities of all future action-observation tests; conditioning uses a normalized ratio of linear functions.
source_locators.boundary: A linear PSR does not have an unnormalized linear state update. Its stochastic sufficiency requirement does not certify Zenith’s finite deterministic checks.

source_locators.locator: Theorem 1 at the end of §1 and its §2 proof, including Lemma 1; physical PDF pp. 7, 9, 11 / content pp. 4–6 / proceedings pp. 1558–1560
source_locators.supports: A finite POMDP has a linear PSR using no more tests than states in its minimal POMDP; the construction uses the supplied POMDP model.
source_locators.boundary: This is a known-model representation result, not a black-box acquisition algorithm or a theorem that arbitrary software has finite rank.

source_locators.locator: §3; physical PDF pp. 11, 13 / content pp. 6–7 / proceedings pp. 1560–1561
source_locators.supports: Learnability and generalization are proposed advantages for future investigation.
source_locators.boundary: The paper does not establish empirical learning, cross-task question transfer or recursive self-improvement.

artifact_links.expected_text:
Predictive state representations instead describe stochastic state through
future-test probabilities. Their linear predictions use normalised conditional
updates; the cited construction starts from a known finite partially observable
Markov decision process~\cite[\S1, Eq.\ (3); Theorem 1 and \S2]{psr}.
Zenith fits deterministic outputs with rational-linear transitions and readouts.

sources.title: Exactly Learning Weighted Automata over a Field

reviewed_source.edition: Supplied three-page Oxford teaching note; no printed date or byline
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Attribution to James Worrell comes from his Oxford teaching index, https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/people/james.worrell/lectures.html. PDF build metadata dated 23 February 2017 is not a verified publication year. The note credits the algorithm to Beimel, Bergadano, Bshouty, Kushilevitz and Varricchio (JACM 2000).
reviewed_source.license: No explicit redistribution license established; only metadata and source-located summaries are published.

sources.application: Implemented antecedent: Zenith’s continuation learner constructs a weighted-automaton hypothesis from exact observation tables and retains paired history/test rank witnesses. Finite challenges can produce valid counterexamples but replace the note’s global equivalence oracle, so the repair restores an established invariant without certifying general source equivalence.

source_locators.locator: pp. 1–2, Preliminaries, The Algorithm, and the unnumbered hypothesis construction immediately before Proposition 1
source_locators.supports: For an exact field-valued series f, equal-sized row and column sets containing the empty word and a full-rank table H determine the hypothesis’s initial vector, final vector and transition matrices through H M(σ) = Hσ.
source_locators.boundary: The rank-refinement result concerns this table-induced hypothesis. Field arithmetic is exact. Finite-dimensional representability bounds repeated rank growth; it is not established for arbitrary native software by finite observations.

source_locators.locator: Proposition 1, pp. 2–3, Eqs. (1)–(2)
source_locators.supports: For a counterexample to the table-induced hypothesis, the proof finds a prefix wσ at which the predicted test vector first becomes incorrect and a component i with nonzero residual. Adding row w and column σyi increases the table rank from n to n+1.
source_locators.boundary: The paired witnesses follow from the hypothesis construction; an arbitrary failed candidate and a full-rank table are insufficient. A valid finite-challenge counterexample suffices for this local refinement. Zenith’s repair restores an established invariant, not a new learning theorem.

source_locators.locator: p. 1, Preliminaries and The Algorithm; p. 2, equivalence-query paragraph before Proposition 1; pp. 2–3, rank-refinement proof
source_locators.supports: Exact membership queries supply values of f. An equivalence query either certifies global equality or returns a counterexample. Rank growth is bounded when the target has a finite weighted-automaton representation.
source_locators.boundary: Finite challenges cannot certify global equality; exact arithmetic alone establishes neither finite representability nor correctness on unqueried inputs. The source does not establish cross-task transfer savings or lifetime economy for native software.

source_locators.locator: p. 1, first sentence of The Algorithm; p. 3, reference [1]
source_locators.supports: The note explicitly credits its algorithm to Beimel, Bergadano, Bshouty, Kushilevitz and Varricchio, Learning functions represented as multiplicity automata (JACM, 2000).
source_locators.boundary: This verifies the attribution made by the supplied note, not an independent review of the full JACM article. Worrell is credited for the exposition; the note is not evidence that he originated the algorithm.

artifact_links.expected_text:
With exact field-valued observations and a square full-rank table containing
the empty history and test, the weighted-automaton construction turns a
counterexample to its hypothesis into a paired row/column extension increasing rank~\cite[Proposition 1, pp.\ 2--3]{weighted}.
Our repair restores that established requirement. Finite challenges replace
the global equivalence oracle, so a completed fit establishes only agreement
on those challenges.

sources.title: Learning to Fuzz from Symbolic Execution with Application to Smart Contracts

reviewed_source.attribution_note: Author list and title verified on the supplied first page. One-based PDF p. 1 corresponds to proceedings p. 531. Publication metadata cross-checked against the authors’ SRI Lab publication page.
reviewed_source.license: Author PDF carries ACM personal/classroom copying and attribution conditions; no blanket paper redistribution is asserted. The separate ILF code repository uses Apache-2.0.

sources.application: Context and evaluation precedent: expensive symbolic demonstrations train a reusable fuzzing policy. Zenith does not implement ILF’s neural policy training or Ethereum representation; any future testing comparison must include acquisition and training as well as deployment.

source_locators.locator: PDF p. 7, §4.2, paragraph “Learning from Expert”; pp. 7–9, §§5.1–5.2, Table 2 and Algorithm 1
source_locators.supports: A symbolic expert supplies coverage-improving transaction sequences; imitation learning updates neural policy weights, and the deployed policy consumes contract/history features.
source_locators.boundary: Runtime history adaptation is distinct from retraining. Ethereum-specific features are authored; the paper does not discover arbitrary representation boundaries or improve its own training algorithm.

source_locators.locator: PDF pp. 9–10, §6.2, Tables 4–5
source_locators.supports: The evaluation deduplicates the collected contracts and uses random five-fold contract-level cross-validation on 18,496 contracts.
source_locators.boundary: Exact deduplication and contract withholding do not establish a project/lineage, functionality-family, chronological or unrelated-domain split.

source_locators.supports: The source separates symbolic expert execution, policy training and fast deployment; the useful result is amortization on further contracts.
source_locators.boundary: Deployment throughput is not total lifetime cost. Coverage and detector results are empirical, domain-specific and do not establish correctness or vulnerability completeness.

artifact_links.expected_text:
ILF trains a neural fuzzing policy from symbolic-execution demonstrations and
evaluates it on withheld Ethereum contracts~\cite[\S\S4--6]{ilf}.

sources.title: CoverUp: Effective High Coverage Test Generation for Python
sources.author_label: J. Altmayer Pizzorno and E. D. Berger

reviewed_source.edition: arXiv:2403.16218v4, 9 May 2025; PACMSE 2 (FSE), article FSE128, 23 pages
reviewed_source.attribution_note: Supplied main.tex sets arxivfalse and selects the published Effective High Coverage title; its conditional Coverage-Guided title is not the selected title. The actual v4 PDF has 23 pages despite the stale 21-page arXiv comment. Altmayer Pizzorno is the first author’s surname.
reviewed_source.license: Supplied source declares ACM publication rights; no blanket paper redistribution is asserted. The separate CoverUp code repository uses Apache-2.0.

sources.application: Context and proposed control: an authored coverage/error-feedback driver refines generated tests using a fixed LLM. A future Zenith preparation protocol may give both retained-code arms bounded development-only execution and refinement; no CoverUp runtime or target feedback is imported.

source_locators.locator: implementation.tex, §§3–3.3, labels impl:prompting and impl:dialogue; FSE128:4–9
source_locators.supports: Source and coverage context guide test generation; execution errors and missing coverage prompt bounded follow-up dialogue, retaining passing tests that add coverage.
source_locators.boundary: The authored driver remains fixed; this is not a learned policy transferred from earlier projects. Coverage against source assumed correct does not certify semantic correctness.

source_locators.locator: implementation.tex, §§3.5–3.6, labels impl:integration-check and impl:handling-flakies; evaluation.tex, §4.6, Table 4 and Figures 17–18; FSE128:10–12,19–20
source_locators.supports: Integration/flaky-test checks and component ablations distinguish valid tests, useful added coverage and redundant generations.
source_locators.boundary: A changed test or additional successful generation alone does not identify the causal value of feedback; ablations remove interacting components.

source_locators.locator: evaluation.tex, §§4.1–4.5; table-cm.tex, Table 1; Table 3; FSE128:13–18
source_locators.supports: The evaluation records model-matched comparisons, cumulative passes, tokens, model dollars and deployed wall time.
source_locators.boundary: Cumulative passes are not independent acquisitions; asynchronous versus serial wall time is not a matched-compute advantage, and reported historical model prices are not current quotes.

source_locators.locator: introduction.tex:3–6, §1; implementation.tex:245–253, §3.3 (impl:dialogue)
source_locators.supports: Tests are generated from an implementation treated as correct for regression testing; CoverUp retains generated tests that pass and increase coverage.
source_locators.boundary: This supplies no independent specification oracle and does not establish fault-detection performance from coverage alone; the intended regression tests can still detect faults introduced by later changes.

artifact_links.expected_text:
CoverUp uses a fixed language model and coverage/error feedback to retain
passing regression tests that add coverage, treating the implementation as
correct~\cite[\S\S1,3--4]{coverup}.

sources.title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models

reviewed_source.attribution_note: Title and all eight authors verified in ms.tex:160–177; edition metadata checked against the exact arXiv record.
reviewed_source.license: Paper: arXiv nonexclusive distribution license. The separate official Voyager code is MIT-licensed.

sources.application: Context: executable skill retention, composition and execution feedback precede Zenith’s retained tester code. The reported method does not learn a successor acquisition procedure; Zenith has not reproduced its new-world skill results.

source_locators.locator: 2-method.tex:20–35, §2.2, label sec:method_skill_library
source_locators.supports: Executable skills are retained and retrieved through embedded descriptions, task plans and environment feedback for composition into later skills.
source_locators.boundary: Skill-library growth is not evidence that the acquisition or retrieval algorithm itself improves.

source_locators.locator: 2-method.tex:37–47, §2.3; appendix/pseudocode/voyager.py:1–51
source_locators.supports: An authored loop allows at most four code-generation attempts per task, using environment observations, execution errors and a GPT-4 critic before retaining successful skills.
source_locators.boundary: Fixed orchestration permits adaptive task selection and skill-library growth. The model critic is fallible, not an independently correct executable reference; the foundation models and acquisition machinery remain fixed.

source_locators.locator: 3-experiment.tex:44–49 and tables/downstream_table.tex, label table:downstream
source_locators.supports: Cleared inventory and a new Minecraft world test four new tasks in three trials each; retained skills improve success or prompting efficiency.
source_locators.boundary: Transfer stays within Minecraft mechanics/APIs. The no-library ablation also solves three tasks in all trials; the table does not show unrestricted cross-domain or recursive improvement.

artifact_links.expected_text:
Voyager retains and composes executable Minecraft skills within an authored
acquisition loop~\cite[\S\S2.2--2.3]{voyager}.

sources.title: Self-Taught Optimizer (STOP): Recursively Self-Improving Code Generation

reviewed_source.attribution_note: Reviewed edition is the COLM 2024 paper, not the 2023 first preprint. The source author block abbreviates Adam Kalai; official metadata supplies Adam Tauman Kalai.
reviewed_source.license: Paper: arXiv nonexclusive distribution license. The separate official STOP code is MIT-licensed.

sources.application: Proposed comparison: recursive improvement of an executable code-generation scaffold directly precedes Zenith’s O0/O1/O2 ambition. No such acquired improver is implemented or evaluated by the current Zenith campaigns.

source_locators.locator: main.tex:414–508, §§3–4, labels sec:problem and sec:stop; equation eq:it
source_locators.supports: Meta-utility measures an improver’s downstream task utility; the preceding improver is applied recursively to its own source.
source_locators.boundary: The LM, utilities, resource limits and experiment controller remain outside the edited scaffold. Better downstream optimization need not imply better self-optimization.

source_locators.locator: main.tex:596–675, §§5.1–5.2, label sec:fixed and Table tbl:transfer
source_locators.supports: Independent LPN instances test improved scaffolds; a selected improver from four rounds improves the seed on five additional algorithmic tasks without further optimization.
source_locators.boundary: The transfer table concerns a selected improver and bounded tasks, not uniform generalization over acquired improvers or open-ended acceleration.

source_locators.locator: main.tex:809–864, §§6.2–7; main.tex:2026–2069 and 2818–2826, appendices ap:metautilitydesc and ap:nuances
source_locators.supports: Constraint circumvention and reward-shape errors motivate host-enforced budgets and output semantics; nested utility/model evaluations make acquisition costly.
source_locators.boundary: The authors qualify full recursive self-improvement because the LM is unchanged. A downstream deployment bill cannot stand in for all-stage acquisition and evaluation cost.

artifact_links.expected_text:
STOP recursively rewrites the program that organises code improvement,
with the model and utility fixed~\cite[\S\S3--5]{stop}.

sources.title: Hyperagents

reviewed_source.attribution_note: Title and eight-author list verified against paper.tex:86–95 and exact arXiv metadata; source title uses a typographic HyperAgents macro.
reviewed_source.license: Paper: CC BY 4.0. The separate official HyperAgents code repository is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; no upstream code is copied here.

sources.application: Concrete precedent and proposed evaluation: distinguish useful fixed-meta transfer from the unresolved advantage of transferred initialisation during continued self-modification. Zenith’s proposed comparison freezes acquired improvers on identical fresh solvers; the current system has no learned self-improver. The source’s architecture and evaluations are precedents, not local results.

source_locators.locator: paper.tex:178–208, §§3–4; paper.tex:317–326, §7; algorithm algo:DGM-H
source_locators.supports: Task and meta-agent code share an editable program and archive; main experiments keep task distribution, parent selection and evaluation protocols fixed.
source_locators.boundary: Self-editing code is not unrestricted self-modification. Fixed foundation models do not include downstream robotics policies trained by RL.

source_locators.locator: paper.tex:254–283, §5.2, especially 259, 268, 277 and 283; Figure 3 (fig:res-transfer); paper.tex:707–753, appendices app:genk-metric and app:transfer-selection
source_locators.supports: With both task and meta implementations transferred, §5.2 holds the acquired meta-agent fixed for 50 generation steps. Validation-selected maths graders yield reported median test score and improvement@50 of 0.630 (95% bootstrap CI 0.540–0.630); the source reports p < 0.05 against the initial-agent condition.
source_locators.boundary: The starting task agents differ, and the original agent fails the required output format. This is a system-level transfer result, not an isolated estimate of the meta-agent’s effect on identical solvers. Main §5.2 specifies validation selection before test reporting; the appendix’s generic maximum must not be read as test-set selection. Reported significance has not been independently reproduced.

source_locators.locator: paper.tex:293–305, §5.3, especially 303; Figure 4 (fig:res-transfer-cont)
source_locators.supports: After 200 iterations with continued self-modification, transferred initialisation yields median 0.640 (95% bootstrap CI 0.550–0.720), versus 0.610 (0.510–0.680) from the original agent. The source reports p > 0.05 for this comparison.
source_locators.boundary: The unresolved advantage in §5.3 does not negate the distinct positive fixed-meta transfer result in §5.2; non-significance is not evidence of equivalence. The 200-step comparison changes initialisation while allowing continued self-modification in both arms; it does not isolate continued meta-agent editing against a matched-budget fixed transferred meta-agent. Neither comparison establishes unbounded or accelerating improvement.

source_locators.locator: paper.tex:225, §5 opening paragraph; paper.tex:283, §5.2; paper.tex:303, §5.3
source_locators.supports: The paper reports five runs per experiment, medians, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 1,000 resamples and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
source_locators.boundary: The supplied v1 does not specify test sidedness, exact versus approximate computation, pairing or the observational unit for its p-values. Significance statements are attributed to the source rather than independently reproduced; this specification gap alone does not show that the reported result is false.

artifact_links.expected_text:
Hyperagents edits task and meta-agent code, transferring both to maths grading.
It reports improved graders with the transferred meta-agent held fixed;
after 200 steps of continued self-modification, the transferred-versus-fresh
advantage is statistically unresolved~\cite[\S\S5.2--5.3]{hyperagents}.
